name: Song of Songs
sourceNote: Written freshly, thought for thought, from the oldest Hebrew, Greek, and Aramaic witnesses (the Masoretic Text with the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint, and the Samaritan Pentateuch). © 2026 Jose Santiago. All rights reserved.

verses.text: The Song of Songs,{a} written by Solomon.{b}

“Let him kiss me with kisses from his mouth,{c}
because your love{d} is better than wine.

Your perfumes smell wonderful.
Your name is like perfume poured out.
No wonder the young women adore you.

Take me with you. Let us hurry!
The king has led me into his rooms.”
“We will be glad and celebrate with you.{e}
We will praise your love above wine.”
“They are right to adore you.”

“Though my skin is dark, I am lovely,
young women of Jerusalem.
I am as dark as the tents of Kedar{f}
and as the tent curtains of Solomon.

Please do not gaze at my dark skin.
The sun scorched me.
My brothers were angry with me,
and they sent me to guard their vineyards.
My own vineyard, I did not guard.

Tell me, you who hold my heart,
where do you graze your sheep?
Where do they rest at midday?
Why should I be left wandering like a veiled woman{g}
near your friends’ flocks?”

“Do you not know,
loveliest of all women?
Then follow the sheep’s trail
and let your young goats feed
beside the shepherds’ tents.{h}

My dearest, you remind me
of a mare in Pharaoh’s team of chariot horses.{i}

Your cheeks are lovely between your earrings,
and your neck is lovely among your strings of beads.

We will make you gold earrings
decorated with silver.{j}

While the king was resting at his table,
my perfume{k} filled the air with its smell.

To me, the one I love is a small bag of myrrh{l}
resting all night between my breasts.

To me, the one I love is a bunch of henna flowers{m}
in the vineyards of En-gedi.{n}

My dearest, you are so beautiful!
Yes, so beautiful, with eyes like doves.”{o}

“How handsome you are, my love, and how charming!{p}
Our bed is green with leaves.

The beams of our house are cedar,
and our ceiling is made of juniper wood.{q}

notes.text: This is a Hebrew way of saying “the best song.”
Or “for Solomon” or “about Solomon.” The name Solomon is tied to the word shalom, “peace.”
The woman speaks in verses 2–4. The Hebrew has no labels for who is speaking, so they are guessed from the grammar here and below.
Hebrew dodim, “lovemaking” or “caresses.” It also appears in verse 4. The Septuagint reads the same letters differently and says “your breasts.”
The “we” may be the young women of verse 3, or friends. The word “you” is male.
Kedar was a desert tribe of Syria and Arabia. The name may mean “dark.” Their tents were made of black goat hair.
She may be veiled like a woman who sells herself (compare Genesis 38:14–15). Some old copies say “a woman who wanders.”
He answers in verse 8, or it may be the friends.

He speaks in verses 9–11. The Hebrew word rayati means “my companion,” and it is his usual name for her in this song. A mare set loose among stallions pulling chariots was a well-known picture of distraction.
The “we” here may be his companions or the friends.
She speaks in verses 12–14. Hebrew nard, or spikenard, was a costly perfume made from a plant of the Himalayas.
Myrrh is a sweet-smelling tree sap from Arabia and East Africa. People wore it in a small pouch.
Henna is a shrub with sweet-smelling bunches of white flowers. It was also used for dye.
En-gedi means “spring of the young goat.” It was an oasis on the west shore of the Dead Sea.
He speaks.
She speaks in verses 16–17. Some people split verse 17 between the two speakers.
Or “firs” or “cypresses.” The exact tree is uncertain.

verses.text:
“I am a wildflower{a} from the plain of Sharon,{b}
a lily blooming in the valleys.”

“Among thorns, a lily stands out,
and so does my dearest among the other young women.”{c}

“Among the forest trees, an apple tree{d} stands out,
and so does my love among the young men.{e}
I am happy to rest in his shade,
and his fruit is sweet in my mouth.

He brought me to the banquet hall,
and his flag over me is love.

Give me raisin cakes to make me strong.
Give me apples to refresh me,
because I am weak with love.

His left hand is under my head,
and his right arm holds me close.

I make you promise, women of Jerusalem,
by the gazelles and the deer of the field:
do not stir up love or wake it
until the right time.{f}

Listen! It is the one I love!
Look, here he comes,
leaping over the mountains,
bounding across the hills.

The one I love is like a gazelle
or a young deer.
See him waiting outside our wall,
gazing in through the windows,
looking through the lattice.

My love speaks, and this is what he says:
‘Rise, my dearest,
my lovely one, and walk with me.

Look, the winter is over.
The rains have stopped and gone away.

Flowers are coming up in the land.
The time for singing{g} has come.
The sound of doves cooing
is heard in our country.

The fig tree is ripening its early fruit,
and the grapevines in bloom smell sweet.
Rise, my dearest,
my lovely one, and walk with me.

My dove, hiding in the rocky cracks,
in the secret places of the cliff,
let me look at you.
Let me hear you speak,
for your voice is pleasant
and you are lovely to see.’

Chase away the foxes for us,{h}
the little foxes
that wreck the vineyards,
while our grapevines are in bloom.

I belong to my love, and he is mine.
He feeds his flock among the lilies.

Before the evening breeze comes
and the shadows flee,
return, my beloved, like a gazelle
or a young deer
bounding over the rocky hills.”{i}

notes.text: The flower is uncertain. It may be a crocus, narcissus, or other meadow flower. The Septuagint says “a flower of the plain.” The woman speaks.
Sharon was the coastal plain south of Mount Carmel, known for pastures and wildflowers. The name means “plain.”
He speaks.
Hebrew tappuach. It may be an apple, apricot, or quince.
She speaks in verses 3–17.

This is a word game. The Hebrew words for “gazelles” and “deer of the field” sound like the titles “Yahweh of Armies” and “God Almighty” (El Shaddai), as if she is making the promise in a hidden way. The Septuagint says “by the powers and the strengths of the field.”
Or “pruning,” as in the Septuagint. The Hebrew word zamir can mean either.
It is not clear who speaks verse 15. She may be quoting a song, or her brothers may be speaking (compare 1:6).
Or “the mountains of Bether,” a place nobody knows, or “the mountains of spices” (compare 8:14). The Septuagint says “the mountains of the ravines.”

verses.text:
‘Let me get up and walk through the town,
along the streets and the open squares,
and search for the man my heart loves.’
I searched, and could not find him.

The night guards found me
as they made their rounds in the town.
‘Did you happen to see the man my heart loves?’

I had just passed them
when I found the man my heart loves.
I grabbed him and would not release him
until I had brought him to my mother’s house,
into the room where she gave birth to me.

Women of Jerusalem, I want your promise,
sworn by the gazelles and by the deer of the field:
never stir up love or wake it
before it is ready.”

Look, it is the carriage of Solomon!
Sixty soldiers surround it,
chosen from the soldiers of Israel.

Each of them grips a sword.
They are trained for war.
Each one wears his sword on his hip
to guard against night terrors.

King Solomon had a carriage{d} built for himself
out of timber from Lebanon.{e}

He had silver posts put in,
and a gold back.
The seat was covered with purple cloth,
and the inside was decorated lovingly{f}
by the women of Jerusalem.

Come out, women of Zion,
and look at King Solomon
wearing the crown his mother put on him
on his wedding day,
the day his heart was glad.

notes.text: She speaks in verses 1–5. Literally “in the nights.”
It is not said who speaks verses 6–11. It may be the friends, or a storyteller. The words “Who is this” are female in Hebrew, so they may mean the carriage or the bride.
Frankincense is a white tree sap from southern Arabia and Somalia. People burned it as incense.
Hebrew appiryon. It is found only here. It may be a Persian or Greek word for a carrying chair.
Lebanon means “white,” from its snowy mountain tops. It was famous for cedar trees.
Or “decorated with leather,” from a related word. The Hebrew is uncertain.

verses.text:
Your teeth are like a flock of sheep
just washed after being sheared.
Each one has a twin,
and not one is missing.

Your lips are a thread of red,
and your speech is charming.
Behind the veil, your cheeks
are like pomegranate halves.

Your neck is like David’s tower,
built in layers of stone,{c}
hung with a thousand shields,
the round shields of mighty soldiers.

Your breasts are like twin fawns,
young gazelles
that feed among the lilies.

Before the evening breeze comes
and the shadows flee,
I will go to the hill of myrrh
and the mountain of incense.

You are beautiful in every way, dearest.
You have no fault at all.

You have captured my heart, my sister,{f} my bride.
One glance from your eyes captured it,
one pearl on your necklace.

How sweet your love is, my sister, my bride!
Your love is far better than wine,
and the scent of your perfumes beats every spice.

Sweetness like the honeycomb falls from your lips, my bride.
Honey and milk lie under your tongue,
and your clothing carries the smell of Lebanon’s cedars.

My sister, my bride, you are a locked garden,
a spring{g} shut up, a fountain sealed.

Your growing plants are an orchard{h} of pomegranates
with the best fruits,
henna and nard,

You are a fountain that waters gardens,
a well of fresh water,
a stream running down from Lebanon.”

“Wake up, north wind!
Come here, south wind!{l}
Blow across my garden,
and let its fragrance drift out.
Let my love enter his own garden
and eat its finest fruit.”

notes.text: He speaks in verses 1–15.
Gilead was the hill country east of the Jordan River, known for its pastures. The name may mean “pile of witness” (compare Genesis 31:47–48).
Hebrew talpiyyoth. It is found only here and its meaning is uncertain. It may mean “in rows of stone,” “for weapons,” or “as a landmark.”
The Septuagint says “Come from Lebanon, my bride.” The Hebrew “with me” can be read as “come” with a small change in vowels.

Amana was a peak in the Anti-Lebanon mountains. Senir was the Amorite name for Hermon (Deuteronomy 3:9), or a nearby peak. Hermon is the highest mountain in the area, about 9,200 feet (2,814 meters) tall.
“Sister” was a loving name for a beloved or bride in love poems of the ancient Near East. It does not mean she is a relative.
Hebrew gal, which may mean “pool” or “spring.” The Septuagint and some other old copies read gan, “garden,” repeating the first line.
Hebrew pardes, “park” or “orchard” (compare Ecclesiastes 2:5).
Saffron is made from the dried middle parts of the crocus flower. People used it as a spice and a dye.
Hebrew qaneh, a sweet-smelling reed or cane brought in from the east (compare Exodus 30:23).
Here “aloes” means eaglewood, a sweet-smelling wood from Asia. It is not the aloe plant used as medicine.
She speaks in verse 16.

verses.text:
“I have come to my garden, my sister,{a} my bride.
I have gathered my myrrh and spices.
I have eaten my honeycomb and honey.
I have drunk my wine and milk.”
“Eat, friends, and drink!
Drink all you want, lovers.”{b}

“I was sleeping, yet my heart stayed awake.{c}
Listen! My love is tapping at the door:
‘Let me in, my sister, my dearest,
my dove, my perfect one.
Dew has soaked my head,
and the night mist has dampened my curls.’

‘I have already taken off my robe.
Why dress again?
I have washed my feet.
Why dirty them?’

My love reached his hand through the opening in the door,{d}
and my heart pounded for him.

I rose to unlock the door for my beloved.
Myrrh dripped from my hands,
pure myrrh ran from my fingers,
onto the door bolt.

I opened to my beloved,
but he had already turned and gone.
My heart sank when he had spoken.{e}
I hunted for him and could not find him.
I cried out his name, but no answer came.

The watchmen on patrol in the city found me.
They beat me and bruised me.
The wall guards
pulled off my cloak.

Women of Jerusalem, I beg you:
when you find my beloved,
what will you say to him?
Say that I am sick with love.”

“How is your beloved better than other men,{f}
most beautiful of women?
How is he better than other men,
that you ask this of us?”

“My beloved glows with health,{g}
and he is the best among ten thousand men.

His eyes are like doves
by flowing streams,
bathed in milk
and set like gems.{i}

His cheeks are like gardens of spice,
like banks of sweet perfume.{j}
His lips are like lilies
dripping with pure myrrh.

His legs are marble pillars
standing on gold bases.
He looks as grand as Lebanon,
as tall as the cedar trees.

His mouth is all sweetness.
Everything about him is lovely.
That is the man I love and my friend,
women of Jerusalem.”

notes.text: He speaks in the first four lines.
Or “drink deeply of love.” It is not clear who speaks these two lines: the friends, a storyteller, or he himself.
She speaks in verses 2–8, telling about a dreamlike night. He speaks in verse 2, and she answers in verse 3.
Literally “through the hole,” probably the keyhole or latch opening of the door.
Or “when he turned away.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
The women of Jerusalem speak in verse 9.
She answers in verses 10–16. Hebrew tsach, “bright” or “shining.”
Hebrew taltallim. It is found only here. It may mean “like palm branches” or “curly.”
Or “sitting by full pools.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
This follows the Hebrew text. The Septuagint and some other old copies say “pouring out perfumes,” with a change of vowels.
Tarshish was a faraway port, maybe in Spain. Here it probably means a gem named for it, such as beryl or topaz.
Literally “sapphires.” The ancient stone with this name was probably lapis lazuli.

verses.text:
“Which way did your beloved go,{a}
loveliest of women?
Where has he turned,
so we can search for him with you?”

“My beloved has gone to his own garden,{b}
to the spice beds,
to tend his flock there
and gather lilies.

He is mine, and I am his.
His flock feeds among the lilies.”

Look away from me,
because your eyes overpower me.
Your hair is like a herd of goats
spilling down from Gilead.

Your teeth are like a flock of ewes
climbing out of the pool after a washing.
Every ewe has twin lambs,
and not one has lost hers.

Behind your veil, your cheeks
look like pomegranate halves.

There may be sixty queens,
eighty other wives,
and countless young women,

But my dove, my flawless one, has no equal.
Her mother had no other daughter,
and she is that woman’s treasure.
Young women saw her and said she was blessed.
Queens and other wives gave her praise:

‘Who is this woman, shining like the dawn,
as lovely as the moon,{e}
as bright as the sun,
as stunning as an army with its flags?’”

“I walked down to the nut orchard{f}
to see what was growing in the valley,
to see if the grapevines had sprouted
and the pomegranate trees had bloomed.

Before I knew it, my longing had set me
in the chariot of my noble people.{g}

notes.text: The women of Jerusalem speak in verse 1.
She speaks in verses 2–3.
He speaks in verses 4–10. Tirzah means “she is pleasing.” It was a beautiful city and early capital of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 14:17; 16:23). The Septuagint translates the name as “Pleasure.”
Or “as the stars in the sky.” The Hebrew word nidgaloth is uncertain. It appears again in verse 10.
The poetic Hebrew words here are levanah, “the white one,” for the moon, and chammah, “the hot one,” for the sun.
It is not clear who speaks verses 11–12. It is probably she, and maybe he.
Or “among the chariots of Amminadib,” as a name meaning “my relative is noble.” The Septuagint has “the chariots of Aminadab.” This verse is one of the hardest to read in the whole book.

In Hebrew this verse is 7:1, and 7:1–13 below are Hebrew 7:2–14. The friends call to her in the first two lines, and she (or he) answers in the last two. Shulammite may mean “woman of Shulem” (perhaps Shunem, as in the Septuagint), or it may be a female form of a name tied to Solomon and shalom.
Or “as she dances the dance of Mahanaim.” Mahanaim was a town east of the Jordan River whose name means “two camps” (Genesis 32:2).

verses.text:
Your waist is like a round bowl
that always has spiced wine in it.
Your middle is like a pile of wheat
fenced in with lilies.

Your breasts are like twin fawns,
young gazelles.

How lovely and pleasant you are,
my love, the joy of all joys!{g}

You are as tall as a palm tree,
and your breasts hang like its clusters of dates.

I told myself, ‘Let me climb that palm.
I will take hold of its branches of fruit.’
May your breasts be like clusters of grapes,
and your breath smell like apples,

“To my love I belong,
and I am the one he longs for.

We will rise early and walk to the vineyards
to find out if the grapevines have sprouted,
if their buds have opened,
and if the pomegranate trees have flowered.
I will give you my love there.

The mandrake plants{k} give off their scent,
and at our doors are all the best fruits,
new ones and old ones,
that I have saved for you, my love.”

notes.text: He speaks in verses 1–9a, or the friends speak in verses 1–5. English 7:1–13 is Hebrew 7:2–14.
Literally “daughter of a noble” or “prince’s daughter.”
Heshbon means “reckoning.” It was a city east of the Jordan River, now in the country of Jordan, known for its water pools.
Bath-rabbim means “daughter of many.” It was probably the name of a city gate.
Carmel means “garden land” or “orchard.” It is the tree-covered ridge above the Mediterranean Sea near the modern city of Haifa.
Purple dye, made from the murex shell, was the most costly color in the ancient world.
Or “loved one, daughter of delights,” following some old copies and dividing the Hebrew letters another way.
She takes up his words in the last two lines and speaks in verses 10–13.
This follows the Hebrew text. The Septuagint and some other old copies say “over my lips and teeth.”
Or “in the villages.” Hebrew kefarim can mean either.
Mandrakes are plants with a sweet-smelling yellow fruit. People believed they stirred up love and made families grow (compare Genesis 30:14–16).

subheads.10: She Invites Him to the Countryside

verses.text:
“How I wish you were like a brother to me,{a}
one who nursed at my mother’s breast!
Then I could kiss you in the street,
and nobody would think badly of me.

I would take your hand and lead you
into my mother’s house, and she would teach me.{b}
I would let you drink spiced wine,
the juice of my pomegranates.

His left hand is under my head,
and his right arm holds me close.

Floods of water cannot put out love,
and rivers cannot wash it away.
If someone offered all the wealth in his house to buy love,
people would only laugh at him.”

“We have a little sister,{h}
and she is not grown yet.
What should we do for our sister
on the day someone asks for her hand?

If she is a wall,
we will put a silver tower on top of her.
If she is a gate,
we will lock her in with cedar boards.”

“Run away, my beloved,{o}
and be like a gazelle
or a young deer
on the spice mountains.”

notes.text: She speaks in verses 1–4.
Or, following the Septuagint and some other old copies, “into the room of the one who gave birth to me” (compare 3:4).
This is the same line as in 2:7 and 3:5, but here it leaves out the promise by the gazelles and deer, and it is a question.
The friends speak in the first two lines.
She speaks in verses 5b–7. In the Hebrew, “you” in this verse is male. The Septuagint begins this verse, “Who is this who comes up all in white?”
Or “jealousy.” Hebrew qinah, the strong feeling of love.

Hebrew shalhevetyah. The ending -yah may be the short form of God’s name, “a flame of Yahweh.” It may also only make the word stronger, “a mighty flame,” since Hebrew sometimes uses God’s name that way. This may be the only mention of God in the Song.
Her brothers speak in verses 8–9 (compare 1:6).
She speaks in verses 10–12.
Hebrew shalom. It may be a word game on Solomon (Shelomoh) and the Shulammite (6:13).
Baal-hamon means “owner of plenty” or “lord of a crowd.” Nobody knows where it was. The name may be a symbol.
Hebrew “a thousand of silver,” meaning a thousand shekels. A shekel weighs about 0.4 ounce, so this is about 25 pounds (11.5 kilograms).
Hebrew “two hundred,” meaning two hundred shekels of silver, about 5 pounds (2.3 kilograms).
He speaks in verse 13. “You” is female.
She speaks in verse 14 (compare 2:17).
